newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. says condoms essential in refugee crises.
newsitem.headline: U.N. says condoms essential in refugee crises.

text.p: Relief workers dealing with the outbreak of a refugee crisis should make condom distribution a top priority, according to a U.N. pamphlet on AIDS prevention.

"However much the relief workers may be concentrating on other things, it is very important indeed -- from the earliest possible moment -- to make condoms available, and in sufficient quantities," it said.

The publication, "Refugees and AIDS," was issued by the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS. It contains advice on preventing the spread of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome and HIV, the virus that causes it.

Among factors making HIV such a critical issue for refugees, it says, is the fact that 75 percent of refugees worldwide are women and children. The breakdown of family and social ties loosens traditional values and refugees are particularly vulnerable to sexual coercion, abuse or rape.
Exchanging sex for money to buy food and other essentials is not uncommon, the pamphlet says, noting both men and women refugees are often without their partners.
"Children in refugee camps, with little to occupy themselves, will often start to experiment with sex earlier than children in other situations," it said.

"Prostitution very often becomes established in or around refugee camps. It will inevitably involve both the refugee and host communities. Both sex workers and clients are at high risk of HIV infection if the sexual behaviour practiced is not safe or protected by a condom," it added.

"Where armies are involved and in contact with the refugees, the risks of infection -- through forced or consensual sex -- are often high. Rates of infection among the military are frequently much higher than in the general population."

The pamphlet also noted that if an emergency occurs in an area where intravenous drug use is common this practice may continue in refugee camps, with the sharing of unsterilized needles adding to the risk of transmitting HIV.

Ensuring a safe blood supply is vitally important, though in the acute and often chaotic early stages of an emergency it might be necessary to use HIV tests that are quicker and cheaper but less accurate than sophisticated tests, to screen the blood of potential donors.
To prevent the transmission of HIV, health workers are reminded of the necessity for universal medical precautions, including ordinary soap, disinfectants and various kinds of protective clothing.
